claims.text: Conventional pressureless sintering of single-phase ZrB2 requires temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally pressureless-sintered ZrB2 typically has a coarser grain structure.
Conventionally pressureless-sintered ZrB2 typically has higher residual porosity that increases susceptibility to harsh chemical environments.
SPS can consolidate single-phase ZrB2 at approximately 2100 °C, below the conventional preparation temperature.
SPS applies electrical current and uniaxial pressure simultaneously during ZrB2 consolidation.
Rapid heating and short hold times during SPS limit ZrB2 grain growth.
SPS will produce a refined and more uniformly densified ZrB2 microstructure.
SPS will reduce porosity and grain-boundary defects in ZrB2.
Electrical current and applied pressure in SPS accelerate mass transport and enhance diffusion at lower temperatures.
Accelerated mass transport and enhanced diffusion promote ZrB2 densification.
SPS inhibits exaggerated grain growth and pore coalescence in ZrB2.
Reduced porosity and grain-boundary defects make ZrB2 less prone to liquid infiltration.
Reduced liquid infiltration and fewer defects will lower hole formation and defect-induced failure during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
SPS-prepared ZrB2 will have lower porosity and fewer microstructural holes than conventionally pressureless-sintered ZrB2.
SPS-prepared ZrB2 will have greater strength than conventionally pressureless-sintered ZrB2.
SPS-prepared ZrB2 will resist chemical attack from the liquid plating bath better than conventionally pressureless-sintered ZrB2.
Conventionally produced single-phase ZrB2 has lower long-term chemical and structural stability than SPS-prepared ZrB2.
SPS is known to lower sintering temperatures and improve densification in many ceramics.
The degree of SPS-induced improvement in ZrB2 and its resistance to long-term liquid-plating exposure remain uncertain and require experimental verification.
